content: The lack of utilization of existing trauma registries to support quality improvement (QI) programs has been highlighted in the literature, particularly in the context of trauma care guidelines (Mitchell, Thal, and Wolferth, 1994; 1995). This issue is not confined to low-resource settings; even in high-income countries, there is significant room for improvement in trauma QI programs. For example, a 2006 survey of 161 hospitals in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland assessed compliance with trauma care standards set by the Royal College of Surgeons and the British Orthopaedic Association. The findings revealed gaps in adherence to these standards, underscoring the need for enhanced QI efforts even in well-resourced healthcare systems. The situation is more pronounced in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). A study conducted as part of the Essential Trauma Care Project evaluated trauma care capabilities at 100 healthcare facilities across Ghana, India, Mexico, and Vietnam. This study assessed not only human and physical resources but also administrative mechanisms. Notably, formal trauma-related QI programs and trauma registries with severity adjustment were entirely absent in these settings. Given the low cost and potential benefits of QI activities in strengthening trauma care, there is a strong recommendation to globally upgrade trauma QI efforts. This can be achieved through formal QI programs in larger hospitals or by integrating trauma cases into broader QI initiatives in smaller facilities. Despite the global dearth of trauma QI activities, there are foundational practices, such as morbidity and mortality (M&M) conferences, that can be leveraged. A small survey of 16 hospital directors and trauma service directors from seven countries revealed that most institutions, particularly larger tertiary care facilities, held regular departmental meetings to discuss mortality. However, only a moderate number engaged in multidisciplinary QI activities, and very few conducted system-wide trauma QI reviews. Furthermore, only three of the 16 institutions reviewed the outcomes of these QI activities with external groups, such as the Ministry of Health (Mock, 2007). Nevertheless, the presence of M&M conferences in many large hospitals provides a solid foundation for building more formal and effective trauma QI programs. M&M conferences, also known as deaths and complications conferences, are widely conducted in hospitals worldwide, particularly in those with formal medical specialty departments. Trauma cases are frequently included in these discussions, especially in hospitals with surgical departments. These conferences serve as a peer review process to identify preventable factors contributing to deaths and complications. To optimize their effectiveness, M&M conferences should not only focus on discussing adverse outcomes but also on identifying systemic problems and initiating corrective actions. Regularly scheduled M&M conferences, tailored to the institution's trauma volume, can significantly enhance the quality of trauma care. For hospitals with high trauma volumes, weekly trauma-specific M&M conferences may be appropriate, while those with lower volumes may address trauma-related issues on a monthly basis. Strengthening the procedural aspects of M&M conferences, such as detailed case reviews and follow-up on corrective actions, can improve their utility in identifying and addressing problems in trauma care. Additionally, integrating trauma QI committees into the M&M framework can further enhance the process. Preventable death panel reviews are another valuable QI technique. These reviews assess whether deaths could have been avoided with optimal care and are conducted by multidisciplinary panels of experts. Such reviews have been shown to improve system functioning, particularly in areas such as rapid transport, early assessment, and timely surgical interventions. While subjective in nature, these reviews often serve as a major stimulus for improvements in trauma care. They require minimal resources and rely on readily accessible data, making them a practical tool for assessing and enhancing trauma systems. Data sources may include hospital records, prehospital information, autopsy reports, and trauma registry data, if available. The panel should critically assess each case, identify areas for improvement, and propose corrective actions. Regular follow-up is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of these actions in improving care quality. In conclusion, while significant gaps exist in trauma QI activities globally, foundational practices such as M&M conferences and preventable death reviews provide a starting point for improvement. By enhancing these processes and integrating them into formal QI programs, healthcare systems can address systemic issues, implement corrective actions, and ultimately improve outcomes for trauma patients.
